claims.text: The initial alloy is a pristine, metastable, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
Controlled service-relevant pre-deformation induces local compositional segregation in the alloy.
Controlled service-relevant pre-deformation induces nanoscale precipitates, especially at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary compositional segregation can reduce plasticity and promote intergranular fracture in a high-entropy alloy.
Stress-induced microstructural evolution reduces toughness relative to the as-cast homogeneous state.
High stress, variable strain rate, and possibly moderately elevated temperature are the loading conditions that trigger the proposed segregation and precipitation.
Localized mechanical stresses destabilize the metastable single-phase structure.
Destabilization of the single-phase structure causes nanoscale precipitate nucleation and grain-boundary solute segregation.
The proposed precipitates and segregated grain boundaries impede dislocation mobility.
The proposed precipitates and segregation inhibit ductile mechanisms such as crack bridging.
Suppression of dislocation motion and ductile mechanisms shifts the alloy from toughness-dominated behavior toward brittle fracture.
Pre-deformed specimens will have lower fracture toughness than pristine specimens.
Pre-deformed specimens will undergo less plastic deformation before crack initiation than pristine specimens.
SEM or TEM will reveal enhanced grain-boundary segregation or precipitate formation after pre-deformation.
The as-cast baseline exhibits uniform ductile deformation and high toughness.
Outside the specified high-stress, high-strain-rate, and temperature regime, the pristine ductile behavior may persist.
